fixes.explanation: Good guess, friend, but Abram never mentions animals here. What he says is, "…since I remain childless…" (Genesis 15:2). The thing he's missing is a child, and that's what he puts in front of God.

Yes, friend! Abram says, "…a servant in my household will be my heir." (Genesis 15:3). That's his worry, laid out for God. Then God answers, "This one will not be your heir, but one who comes from your own body will be your heir." (Genesis 15:4).

Yes, baker! God says, "Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able." (Genesis 15:5). He takes Abram outside to do it. I bet most of us would quit counting around star number twelve. My sprinkle jar is easy to count next to that sky.

That's the one, friend. God says, "So shall your offspring be." (Genesis 15:5). Abram has no child at this point, and God points him to the stars. I think that's a lot to take in. The very next verse says, "Abram believed the LORD…" (Genesis 15:6).

Sand is a fair thing to think of, friend, but it isn't in this verse. God says, "Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able." (Genesis 15:5). The picture here is the heavens, and what Abram is told to count is stars.

Flocks are a fair thing to think of, friend, but God never mentions them here. He says, "Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able." (Genesis 15:5). The count is up in the sky, so that's where Abram is sent to look.

Tents are a reasonable guess, baker, but they aren't in this verse. God says, "Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able." (Genesis 15:5). He sends Abram's attention up to the heavens, and the thing to count is stars.

I see why an altar comes to mind, friend, but that's not what happens in this verse. It says, "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness." (Genesis 15:6). What Abram does here is believe.

Priest sounds official, baker, but God never says it here. He says He brought Abram out of Ur "…to give you this land to possess." (Genesis 15:7). One gift is on the table, and it's the land. Plain and simple.

Not this time, baker. The birds of prey do come down on the carcasses, but "…Abram drove them away." (Genesis 15:11). He's out there chasing them off. The answer is False, because Abram doesn't let the birds have the carcasses.

Scattering is a fair thought, friend, but it's not what God says here. He says, "…afterward they will depart with many possessions." (Genesis 15:14). The picture is leaving with a lot, not scattering.

The hard news is about his descendants, friend, who "…will be strangers in a land that is not their own…" (Genesis 15:13). But God says something different about Abram himself: "You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age." (Genesis 15:15). For Abram, the word is peace.

That's right, friend! "…a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves of the carcasses." (Genesis 15:17). They go down the middle, through the path between the halves. Abram laid those halves opposite each other, so that's the way through.

Yes, baker! "On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram…" (Genesis 15:18). Abram had asked, "…how can I know that I will possess it?" (Genesis 15:8). This is what happens that day. A covenant is a solemn promise, and this one is God's.

A new name sounds big, friend, but this passage doesn't have one. It says, "On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram…" (Genesis 15:18). That's what the LORD does when the firepot and torch pass through.
